subject: medicine
title: Acute Bacterial Meningitis: Clinical Signs, CSF, and Empiric Therapy

steps.tx: A life-threatening medical emergency characterised by acute purulent inflammation of the leptomeninges and subarachnoid space is **bacterial meningitis**. Pathogens colonise the nasopharynx, cross mucosal barriers into the bloodstream, and invade the subarachnoid space across the blood-brain barrier, triggering an intense host neutrophilic inflammatory response, cerebral oedema, and raised intracranial pressure.
steps.say: A life-threatening medical emergency characterized by acute purulent inflammation of the leptomeninges is bacterial meningitis. Pathogens colonise the nasopharynx, cross into the bloodstream, and invade the subarachnoid space, triggering an intense neutrophilic response, cerebral edema, and raised intracranial pressure.

steps.tx: The classic clinical triad of acute bacterial meningitis consists of high fever, altered mental status, and marked nuchal rigidity. Physical examination elicits meningeal signs resulting from inflammatory stretching of hypersensitive spinal nerve roots, including resistance to passive neck flexion and involuntary thigh and knee flexion upon passive neck bending, recognized as the **Brudzinski sign**.

left.title: Kernig Sign
points: Patient supine with hip and knee flexed to 90 degrees
Attempted extension of the knee meets resistance
Pain in hamstring muscles from spinal root stretch
Positive when extension angle is < 135 degrees

right.title: Brudzinski Sign
points: Patient supine with legs fully extended
Examiner passively flexes the patient's neck
Involuntary reciprocal flexion of bilateral hips and knees
Reflects meningeal traction on lumbosacral roots

steps.tx: The overall leading bacterial aetiology across all adult age groups is **Streptococcus pneumoniae** (pneumococcus), responsible for over fifty percent of community-acquired cases. Pneumococcal meningitis frequently arises secondary to contiguous spread from acute otitis media, mastoiditis, or sinusitis, and carries the highest mortality and neurological complication rate among all bacterial forms.
steps.say: The overall leading bacterial cause across all adult age groups is Streptococcus pneumoniae, responsible for over half of community-acquired cases. Pneumococcal meningitis frequently arises from otitis media or sinusitis, carrying the highest mortality and complication rate.

steps.tx: In adolescents and young adults residing in close quarters (dormitories, military barracks), an explosive bacterial meningitis is caused by the Gram-negative diplococcus **Neisseria meningitidis** (meningococcus). Fulminant meningococcaemia precipitates petechial and purpuric skin eruptions, disseminated intravascular coagulation, bilateral adrenal haemorrhagic necrosis (Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome), and rapid septic shock.
steps.say: In adolescents and young adults residing in close quarters, an explosive bacterial meningitis is caused by the Gram-negative diplococcus Neisseria meningitidis. Fulminant meningococcaemia precipitates petechial and purpuric skin eruptions, DIC, bilateral adrenal haemorrhage, and rapid septic shock.

steps.tx: Emergency lumbar puncture provides definitive diagnostic cerebrospinal fluid analysis (**CSF analysis**). In acute bacterial meningitis, CSF exhibits marked pleocytosis with thousands of polymorphonuclear neutrophils (frequently over one thousand cells per microlitre), profound hypoglycorrhachia (CSF to serum glucose ratio under 0.4), and markedly elevated CSF protein exceeding one-hundred milligrams per decilitre.
steps.say: Emergency lumbar puncture provides definitive cerebrospinal fluid analysis. In acute bacterial meningitis, spinal fluid demonstrates marked pleocytosis with over one thousand neutrophils per microlitre, marked hypoglycorrhachia with a glucose ratio under 0.4, and elevated protein.

steps.tx: Before performing lumbar puncture, cranial computed tomography must be obtained only if specific risk factors for herniation exist: focal neurological deficits, new-onset seizures, papilloedema, severely depressed consciousness (GCS under ten), or immunocompromised state. Crucially, when CT imaging is required, empiric blood cultures and intravenous **antibiotics** must never be delayed pending imaging results.
steps.say: Before performing lumbar puncture, cranial computed tomography is required only if specific herniation risk factors exist: focal deficits, seizures, papilloedema, coma, or immunocompromise. When imaging is required, empiric blood cultures and antibiotics must never be delayed.

nodes.label: Screen for Focal Deficits, Papilloedema, Coma
Immediate Blood Cultures + IV Ceftriaxone / Vanco

steps.tx: The empiric bactericidal antibiotic backbone for community-acquired bacterial meningitis in immunocompetent adults is high-dose intravenous **ceftriaxone** (two grams every twelve hours) combined with vancomycin (to cover penicillin-resistant pneumococci). Ceftriaxone provides excellent CSF penetration, broad Gram-negative coverage, and potent killing against both Streptococcus pneumoniae and Neisseria meningitidis.
steps.say: The empiric bactericidal antibiotic backbone for community-acquired bacterial meningitis in adults is high-dose intravenous ceftriaxone combined with vancomycin. Ceftriaxone provides excellent CSF penetration, broad Gram-negative coverage, and potent killing against pneumococcus and meningococcus.

steps.tx: In patients older than fifty years, pregnant women, neonates, and immunocompromised hosts, impaired cell-mediated immunity predisposing to rhombencephalitis and meningitis caused by **Listeria monocytogenes** mandates the immediate addition of intravenous ampicillin (two grams every four hours) to the empiric regimen, as cephalosporins possess zero intrinsic activity against Listeria.
